problem: Diffusion-policy navigation models such as NoMaD are trained jointly on static datasets and suffer catastrophic forgetting when trained sequentially across scenes. Generic replay methods use pixel-level or vector features and ignore relational and hierarchical scene structure.
motivation: Robots deployed in open-world settings meet new scenes continually, and retraining on all accumulated data is costly. Pixel or visual features say what is in a scene but not how objects relate. Scene graphs capture the relations, and hyperbolic geometry embeds hierarchies with low distortion, which should give a more diverse, better-separated replay memory.
key_idea: Encode each observation as a VLM-extracted scene graph, embed it with an R-GCN into the Poincaré disk, and manage a clustered replay memory whose centroids use the Karcher mean and whose samples are replaced by hyperbolic distance to the centroid, for continual diffusion-policy navigation.
insight: The progression in Table 1 is TinyER 36.9 Drop, then VisFeat (no scene graph) 35.2, then Euclidean 34.8, then Hyperbolic 28.5. Both the scene-graph representation and the hyperbolic geometry contribute, and the geometry gives the largest jump. Clustering the memory also beats a single buffer at equal size (Fig. 5 cosine similarity). Note that the Euclidean and VisFeat gains over TinyER are small, so most of the benefit comes only in the full combination.
method: Scene graph extraction: Qwen-VL describes each RGB frame and Qwen3-7B parses the description into (subject, relation, object) triples, computed offline once per scene.
R-GCN embedding: relational graph convolution over the triples gives a 128-d graph embedding z_i; weights are fixed and used only for offline embedding.
Poincaré projection: exponential-map-like projection phi(z)=z/(sqrt(c)(||z||+eps))*tanh(sqrt(c)||z||) with fixed curvature c, so richer structures lie farther from the origin.

Dynamic clustering: a new sample is assigned by Euclidean distance to the nearest centroid, or opens a new cluster if the distance exceeds threshold tau and the cluster cap allows; C clusters each with capacity M.

Structure-sensitive update: cluster centroids are Karcher means (a few Riemannian gradient steps); a new sample replaces the member closest to the centroid if it is farther from the centroid in hyperbolic distance, keeping the more structurally diverse samples.
Replay: n samples drawn uniformly across all clusters are mixed with the current batch to fine-tune the NoMaD diffusion policy (replay capacity 1280 samples).

setting.backbone: NoMaD diffusion policy (fine-tuned sequentially) with Qwen-VL + Qwen3-7B (frozen) for triples and R-GCN (fixed) for embeddings
setting.training_data: SACSoN (indoor) and Recon (outdoor) trajectories split into five sequential scenes, 60% train / 40% test per scene; Habitat online evaluation on five Matterport3D scenes; 20 epochs per scene
setting.action_space: predicted waypoint trajectories from the diffusion policy
setting.simulator: Habitat (Matterport3D scenes) for online evaluation; offline trajectory prediction on SACSoN and Recon

numbers.eval_set_note: 40% held-out trajectories per scene; five sequential scene splits (1~A ... 1~E)
numbers.backbone: NoMaD diffusion policy + R-GCN scene graph memory replay
numbers.extra: replay memory of 1280 samples; SR = >90% predicted waypoints align with GT; sequential training, Drop = SR(1~A) - SR(1~E)

numbers.backbone: NoMaD diffusion policy + Euclidean centroid replay
numbers.extra: ablation: Euclidean L2 distance instead of hyperbolic

numbers.eval_set_note: five Matterport3D scenes used in the sequential protocol
numbers.backbone: NoMaD diffusion policy + hyperbolic dynamic cluster memory replay
numbers.extra: sequential continual training; Collision is collisions per meter
numbers.evidence: Table 2 Online Evaluation in Habitat: HyperDCM-Hyp 56.0 48.3 0.17

numbers_note: Benchmarks are custom (not canonical); splits are reported as 'test' by design. Table 1 SR is an offline waypoint-agreement metric rather than true navigation success. Upper bound Joint NoMaD: Drop 6.3 (offline), SR 63.1 in Habitat.
results: On five sequential scenes, HyperDCM-Hyp cuts the forgetting Drop to 28.5 versus 43.3 for no replay and 36.9 for TinyER (the strongest baseline), and gets 41.5 SR at 1~E versus 28.6 for TinyER. In Habitat it reaches SR 56.0 / SPL 48.3 / collision 0.17, versus 39.2 / 38.5 / 0.37 without replay, still short of joint training (63.1 SR). It also keeps per-stage training cost nearly constant.
limitations: Baselines are only classical CL methods (EWC, SI, LwF, TinyER); no diffusion-specific continual learning methods, and the success metric is a waypoint-agreement proxy on small five-scene splits.

Depends on offline VLM/LLM scene-graph extraction and fixed hyperparameters (curvature, threshold), adding preprocessing cost; a substantial gap to joint training remains, and no real-robot experiments are reported.
